lines.text: The three fires meant the King's army had crossed the Senn. Halvard gave it three weeks to reach Kesting Pass. Southern armies, he said, march like cows.
We had glass-steel, and beacons, and Clay Knights. What we didn't have was cavalry. Horses hate the White, and the White hates horses.
Then the white she-wolf went into the Pale one night, and came back at dawn with her family.
Fourteen frost-wolves, each one twice the size of a man, walking out of the trees in a line behind her, as polite as wedding guests.
The Skeld have hunted frost-wolves for a thousand years. And now you want us to ride them?
Yes.
Kell was never much for speeches.
The wolves had come out of the White because something in it was waking, and they wanted somewhere warm. So I claimed them, one by one, and they accepted.
Then they needed names. A name is a whole claim in one breath, and I knew what it would cost. My wards chose the names. I was too tired to argue.
That one is Biscuit. That one is Turnip. And the biggest one is Lady Pudding.
I named a war-wolf Lady Pudding. The fever lasted two days. Nell sat with me the whole time, and whenever she held my hand, it broke a little.
When the naming was done, the frost-wolves woke the way Ash had once. Bigger. Glossier. Smarter than any horse, and far less interested in being ridden.
The Skeld fell off them for a week. Kell fell off Turnip eleven times in one morning. Turnip seemed to enjoy it.
And Ash's own pups, grown nearly to their father's size since the lamp blazed, chose their own riders.
Rook chose Kell. Birk chose Sigrun, a quiet Skeld girl who had never ridden anything. And Tarn, the runt with the flopped ear, walked past every warrior in the north and lay down at Wren's feet.
No. Absolutely not. I'm an archer. Archers stand still.
Tarn rolled over and showed Wren her belly. Wren lasted about four heartbeats.
By the end of the month, the Wolfhound Riders could cross a frozen lake faster than a horse crosses a meadow. Wren shot from Tarn's back at a full run, and hit everything.
Hold still, Wren. Let me look at you.
Five. Not a Tide, not a borrowed night. Five, settled, and yours. For good.
Does it come with more pay?
That night, a bird came to Greyhollow from the south, carrying a letter in a code only one man in the north could read. Fortunately, it was me.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter one hundred and twenty-six, coming soon.
